meta.title: Who really said "Less is more"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mies van der Rohe or Buckminster Fuller. Robert Browning wrote it in "Andrea del Sarto" (1855) — verified against a scan of the first edition.
meta.ogDescription: Robert Browning printed it in 1855. Mies van der Rohe adopted it as a motto; Buckminster Fuller never said it at all.

answer.label: Not Mies or Fuller — actually Robert Browning
answer.authorDates: 1812–1889 · English poet, master of the dramatic monologue
answer.sourceLine: The exact three words are Browning’s, spoken by the painter Andrea del Sarto in the poem of that name: “Well, less is more, Lucrezia! I am judged.” The line is on page 5 of Men and Women, Volume 2 (1855), confirmed against a proofread scan of the first edition. Mies van der Rohe made the phrase a motto but did not coin it, and Buckminster Fuller — whose own phrase was “doing more with less” — is credited with it in error.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Page 5 of the 1855 first edition; cited by Wikiquote as line 70
Andrea del Sarto, addressing his wife Lucrezia — not the poet in his own voice

source.excerpt:
Who strive—you don’t know how the others strive
To paint a little thing like that you smeared
Carelessly passing with your robes afloat,
Yet do much less, so much less, some one says,
(I know his name, no matter) so much less!
Well, less is more, Lucrezia! I am judged.
trail: 1774 — Christoph Martin Wieland’s “Neujahrswunsch” in Der Teutsche Merkur carries “Und minder ist oft mehr,” though German Wikipedia ↗ notes the phrase’s originator is unknown and reads Wieland’s line as an ellipsis, not a paradox.
1855 — Browning prints “Well, less is more, Lucrezia! I am judged.” on page 5 of Men and Women, Volume 2 ↗.
1907–1910 — working on the AEG Turbine Factory in Peter Behrens’s Berlin office, the young Mies hears the phrase for the first time, by his own later account (Detlef Mertins, via Phaidon ↗).
Since — the line becomes modernism’s slogan and attaches itself to Mies, and then to Fuller; both Wikiquote pages ↗ now list it as misattributed.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the proofread scan of the 1855 first edition. Later collected editions punctuate the line slightly differently — Wikiquote’s sourced text reads “Well, less is more, Lucrezia: I am judged.”

author.name: Robert Browning
author.heading: The poet who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1812–1889 · English poet, master of the dramatic monologue
author.bio: Robert Browning spent much of his career out of fashion, writing knotty, talky poems in the voices of other people — painters, bishops, murderers — while his wife Elizabeth Barrett Browning was the famous one in the household. Men and Women (1855), the two-volume collection that contains “Andrea del Sarto,” landed with a thud on first publication and is now considered his best book. His speciality was the dramatic monologue: a character talks, and gives himself away without meaning to. That is exactly what happens in the line everyone now quotes.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: Two famous names carry this line, and neither wrote it. One of them at least used it; the other seems to have been swept in by association.

items.why: Mies used the phrase constantly and it became inseparable from him, but Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗ and credits Browning. Mies himself pointed elsewhere: in a recollection quoted from Detlef Mertins’s monograph Mies, he said “I heard it in Behrens’s office for the first time” while drafting a facade for the AEG Turbine Factory — adding that Peter Behrens “meant it in another way than I use it” (reprint of the Phaidon article ↗).

Wikiquote lists “Less is more” among Fuller’s misattributions ↗ and notes that what belongs to him is the very different “doing more with less” — part of his 1938 coinage ephemeralization ↗, technology’s ability to do “more and more with less and less until eventually you can do everything with nothing.”

items.tag: Close, but not the same phrase
items.why: Wieland’s “Neujahrswunsch,” published in Der Teutsche Merkur in 1774, contains “Und minder ist oft mehr.” German Wikipedia ↗ says the originator of the formulation is unknown and only occasionally attributed to Wieland, and reads his line as an ellipsis rather than the modern paradox.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact English words belong to Robert Browning, who put them in the mouth of a painter in “Andrea del Sarto,” Men and Women, Volume 2 (1855) ↗ — and, in context, they are not a design principle at all.

context.heading: Why the wrong name stuck
lead: It is a rare misattribution where the famous name is half right. Mies van der Rohe really did use “less is more,” over and over, until it became shorthand for an entire century of glass-and-steel building. What he never did was claim to have invented it. In a recollection quoted from Detlef Mertins’s monograph Mies, the architect said flatly: “I heard it in Behrens’s office for the first time.” He was in his early twenties, drafting a factory facade with nothing on it, and his employer looked at the options and said the words — more than half a century after Browning had already put them in print.

Buckminster Fuller has a weaker claim still. His actual contribution to the more-from-less family is ephemeralization, a term he coined in 1938 for technology’s ability to do “more and more with less and less until eventually you can do everything with nothing.” That is a claim about engineering efficiency, not an aesthetic creed. The two ideas got filed under the same heading by quote sites, and Fuller inherited a line he never wrote.
context.detailsSummary: An earlier German near-miss — and why it isn’t quite the same phrase
detailsBody: Wikiquote and German Wikipedia both point to Christoph Martin Wieland’s poem “Neujahrswunsch,” published in Der Teutsche Merkur in 1774, which contains the line “Und minder ist oft mehr” — and less is often more. German Wikipedia is careful about it, saying the creator of the formulation is unknown and that the phrase is only occasionally attributed to Wieland.

It also makes a point worth keeping: Wieland was not writing a paradox. Read in context the line is an ellipsis — being less quick is often more advisable — with the load-bearing words simply left out, rather than the deliberate oxymoron the modern slogan depends on. So Wieland is a precursor in words, not quite in meaning.
context.pull: Mies made it a motto. Browning made it a sentence.

schema.quotationText: Well, less is more, Lucrezia! I am judged.

sourcesVerified.claim: The 1855 first edition of Men and Women, Volume 2 contains, on page 5, the line "Well, less is more, Lucrezia! I am judged." in the poem "Andrea del Sarto, (called 'The Faultless Painter')".

The full poem, transcribed from the 1855 first-edition scan, includes the surrounding lines 'Yet do much less, so much less, some one says, / (I know his name, no matter) so much less! / Well, less is more, Lucrezia! I am judged.'

Wikiquote lists 'Less is more' under Misattributed on the Ludwig Mies van der Rohe page, saying it is 'Actually Robert Browning, from Andrea del Sarto' and that 'Less is often more' was used earlier by Christoph Martin Wieland.

Wikiquote lists 'Less is more' under Misattributed on the Buckminster Fuller page, crediting Browning's 'Andrea del Sarto' (1855) and Wieland's 'minder ist oft mehr' in Der Teutsche Merkur (1774), and noting that 'doing more with less' is part of Fuller's definition of ephemeralization.

Wikiquote's Robert Browning page gives the quotation as sourced to 'Andrea del Sarto', line 70, and notes 'Less is more' is often misattributed to Buckminster Fuller or Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and was used in 1774 by Christoph Martin Wieland. It also gives Browning's dates as 7 May 1812 – 12 December 1889.

Ephemeralization is a term coined by R. Buckminster Fuller in 1938 for technology's ability to do 'more and more with less and less until eventually you can do everything with nothing', referenced to Nine Chains to the Moon (1938).

German Wikipedia states the creator of the formulation is unknown and it is only occasionally attributed to Wieland; quotes 'Und minder ist oft mehr' from the poem 'Neujahrswunsch' published in Der Teutsche Merkur, 1774, fifth volume, p. 4; and argues the line is an ellipsis rather than an oxymoron. It also notes 'less is more' appears in Browning's 1855 'Andrea del Sarto'.

Reprint of the Phaidon article quoting Detlef Mertins's monograph 'Mies': Mies recalled 'I heard it in Behrens's office for the first time,' while making a drawing for a factory facade, that Behrens said 'Less is more', and that 'he meant it in another way than I use it'; Behrens drafted Mies to work on the AEG Turbine Factory in Berlin between 1907 and 1910.

The Phrase Finder identifies Robert Browning's 1855 poem 'Andrea del Sarto' as the first printed source of 'less is more', quoting 'Well, less is more, Lucrezia.', and notes the phrase is often associated with Mies van der Rohe (1886-1969).

Wikipedia's 'Less is more' article states that in architecture the expression is often erroneously attributed to Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and that Browning's 1855 dramatic monologue 'Andrea del Sarto' uses the phrase.
ArchDaily gives Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's dates as 27 March 1886 – 17 August 1969, says his career began in the studio of Peter Behrens, and calls 'less is more' his famous aphorism.
